newsitem.title: USA: RJR bounces back with dividend hike, buyback.
newsitem.headline: RJR bounces back with dividend hike, buyback.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, long embattled over the value its stock, is off the ropes and fighting again after a significant pro-tobacco court decision this week and the demise of Carl Icahn's influence on the company, at least for now.
With Friday's announcement of an increased dividend and share repurchase program, the company's external troubles seem more distant, analysts said.
To be sure, the dividend increase and stock buyback were expected, but the turn of events that ended the week gave a boost to RJR and tobacco companies in general, they said.

On Friday, RJR Nabisco shares dipped 1/8 at 36-5/8, but as recently as August, the stock was languishing around $25 a share. At that time, lawsuits were being filed seemingly every day, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration was launching the regulatory initiatives against tobacco that began Friday.

In addition, Icahn and Bennett LeBow, chairman of Brooke Group Ltd, were accumulating RJR Nabisco stock with vigor in an attempt to unseat the company's board of directors and force a spin-off of its 80.5 percent owned Nabisco Holdings Corp.
On Thursday, however, Icahn said he had liquidated his 19.9 million shares of RJR Nabisco.
Across the country, meanwhile, a federal judge in California tossed out San Francisco's Medicaid recovery suit against the tobacco companies.

From the perspective of RJR and others in the industry, the tobacco litigation environment improved as a result of the dismissal because of the similarities between San Francisco's suit and the other 22 state Medicaid suits, analysts said.
As a result, RJR Nabisco can now get on with the business of selling cigarettes and food with fewer distractions.

"For management, it is sort of back to the basics now -- let's make money for our shareholders and let's return some of it to our shareholders," said Martin Feldman, a tobacco industry analyst at Smith Barney.
Feldman said the urgency of a Nabsico spin-off was diminishing as the parent company's stock price rises and shakes off the severe market discount that was almost entirely related to litigation woes.

With a price in the mid 20's, the capital appreciation of RJR's shares stock after a spinoff would have been about a 75 percent gain, according to Feldman. "Today, the value of a spin-off is more like 32 to 33 percent," he said.

Paine Webber analyst Emanuel Goldman said the company was "reasonably on track" to accomplish the turnaround in shareholder value that Chief Executive Steven Goldstone promised when he took the job in the summer of 1995.
